## Anchor: Melbourne
**Dataset** — [Pedestrian Counting System](https://data.melbourne.vic.gov.au/explore/dataset/pedestrian-counting-system-monthly-counts-per-hour/) (City of Melbourne open data): hourly foot-traffic counts from 60–100+ street sensors since May 2009 — one of the world's longest-running urban sensing programs, CC BY 4.0, no login (full 2009–2022 history ships as an archive ZIP on the dataset page; recent data via the live API). *Verified June 2026.*
:::

Look up from the right street corners in central Melbourne and you can find them: small housings on poles and awnings, counting. Each sensor records how many pedestrians pass below, every hour, and has done so — at the oldest sites — since May 2009. The city publishes the ledger freely. It is a modest instrument by the standards of the sensed city, no cameras recognizing faces, no phones traced through the mall; just counts, hour upon hour, sixteen years deep.

Modesty is its virtue. Within this one table live the questions machine learning was built for. *How many people will pass Town Hall at noon next Tuesday?* — prediction. *Which streets behave alike?* — structure. *Did something strange happen last night?* — anomaly. And because the record runs continuously from 2009 through a pandemic that emptied these same streets for months, the dataset carries its own stress test: the most violent regime change any urban sensor network has recorded, sitting in the middle of the training data like a fault line through bedrock.

This chapter is the book's machine-learning survey, and it is organized around those questions in that order. The methods are general; the discipline — what to feed a model, how to score it without flattering it, when to believe it — is where city data differs from the textbook kind, and where this chapter earns its place.

## Two cultures

In 2001 the statistician Leo Breiman, who had left Berkeley for consulting and returned converted, accused his own field of answering the wrong question. Statistics, he argued, had organized itself around *explaining* — fitting interpretable models and reading their coefficients as claims about the world — while a second culture, machine learning, optimized for *predicting*: whatever function best maps inputs to outputs, interpretation be damned. The cultures share equations and differ in loyalty. A regression can serve either; the difference is whether you grade it on its story or on its forecasts.

Cities need both cultures, usually on the same morning. The transport agency timing tram frequencies needs foot-traffic *forecasts* and could not care less why Thursday resembles Wednesday; the council weighing a late-night trading law needs the *why*, because the law operates on causes. Confusing the two is not a technicality. A model that predicts brilliantly can mislead completely about mechanism — and a chapter of this book (@sec-causal) exists because the reverse error, mistaking explanation for licence to predict, has its own body count in policy.

This chapter works in the predictive culture. Its standard of truth is *generalization*: performance on data the model has never seen. Everything else — the algorithms, the features, the diagnostics — is in service of that standard, and most of what goes wrong in applied machine learning goes wrong by accidentally grading a model on data it had already met. Hold that thought through @sec-ml-honest, where it becomes the chapter's sharpest lesson.

## Predicting a street

Forecasting is the licensing exam of the predictive culture, and we will sit it on one well-behaved patient: a high-traffic sensor with a long, mostly unbroken record. <!-- TODO:data — name the chosen sensor and its vital statistics --> The task: given everything through last week, predict every hour of next week.

Two decisions precede any algorithm, and both matter more than the algorithm.

**The features.** Foot traffic is overwhelmingly a function of *when*: hour, weekday, month, public holiday. To these calendar facts we add the series' own memory — the count at this hour last week, yesterday's total — because the recent past is the cheapest oracle available. We deliberately exclude weather, not because it is unimportant (rain visibly dents these counts) but because honest weather *forecasts* are what a deployed model would have, and pretending we had perfect ones would flatter every score that follows. The omission is a confession; Exercise 4 invites you to do better, honestly.

**The baseline.** Before any learning, a rule of thumb: *predict the count from this hour last week.* Seasonal persistence, the forecaster's null hypothesis.

<!-- TODO:data — results table + prose. Expected arc: persistence is embarrassingly strong; ridge ties or trails it; trees beat it by a real but humble margin. State actual MAEs and the % improvement. -->

A model earns its keep by beating a rule of thumb, and urban rules of thumb are strong. Cities are creatures of habit; *last Tuesday* is a forecast that costs nothing and already explains most of next Tuesday. The gradient-boosted trees do beat it — they can see holidays coming, persistence cannot — but the margin is measured in percent, not magnitudes, and a practitioner who reports only their model's error, never the baseline's, is composing fiction with extra steps.

```{python}

```

What did the model learn? Permutation importance — scramble one feature, watch the error — gives the blunt answer:

```{python}
#| label: fig-importance
#| fig-cap: "Permutation importance for the boosted model. The lag features dominate: mostly, the model has learned to consult last week."
#| code-fold: true
# TODO:data — permutation importance on the test window
```

Read importance plots the way you read a witness: for what they saw, not why it happened. *Important* here means *predictively load-bearing for this model on this street* — not causal, not transferable, not policy advice. The lag features dominating is the plot's way of agreeing with the baseline: memory is most of the signal, calendar handles the exceptions. When @sec-causal needs to know what *causes* foot traffic, none of this machinery will be admissible; that is not a flaw but a jurisdiction.

Note what was *not* used: no land-use map, no zoning table, no knowledge of where the bars are. The clusters recover the city's functional anatomy from rhythm alone — and where a sensor lands in a surprising cluster, that is not an error to be smoothed away but the analysis's first interesting sentence. Unsupervised learning generates hypotheses, not findings. The findings come when a surprise survives a second dataset.

## The day the streets stopped

On a Friday in March 2020, the State of Victoria declared a state of emergency, and over the following weeks the sensors recorded something no urban instrument had seen at this resolution: a great city's foot traffic falling toward zero and staying there. Melbourne would eventually endure six lockdowns — among the longest cumulative confinements of any city on earth — and every one of them is written in this table, hour by hour.

For the anomaly detector, this is the rare luxury of labeled catastrophe. The method is deliberately plain: model each sensor's *expected* hour from its own trailing weeks, score each observed hour by its distance from expectation in robust units, and average across the network into a single daily index of strangeness.

<!-- TODO:data — table or prose of top-10 anomalous days; expected mix: lockdown starts/ends, New Year's Eve, AFL Grand Final, White Night, possibly a storm; tell the best non-obvious one -->

Two species of strangeness appear, and the distinction matters more than the detection. An *outlier* is a day that breaks the pattern and releases it — the Grand Final empties the streets it does not border, and Monday returns as if nothing happened. A *regime change* is a day after which the old expectation is simply wrong; March 2020 is the type specimen. Detectors built on trailing baselines will flag a regime change loudly for a few weeks and then, having absorbed the new normal into the baseline, fall silent — the statistical equivalent of growing accustomed to the smell. Knowing which species you face determines whether the right response is to investigate a day or to retire a model.

The pandemic also quietly sabotaged the previous section, and it is worth saying so. Any forecasting model trained across 2020–21 has eaten two years that contradict the other fourteen; any clustering of *average* profiles has averaged a street's before and after. The chapter's analyses dodged this — windows chosen after the recovery, profiles from settled years — but the dodge was a *choice*, made by a human who knew the history, not by the algorithm. The most consequential modeling decisions in this chapter never touched the model.

## Honest evaluation {#sec-ml-honest}

Everything above reported scores on held-out data. This final section is about how easy it is to hold data out and still cheat.

*Leakage*: information unavailable at prediction time finding its way into training. The definition sounds avoidable by inspection. It is not, because the standard tool — random cross-validation — commits it silently on any data with structure in time or space. Shuffle hourly observations into random folds and the model trains on Tuesday 3 p.m. while "predicting" Tuesday 2 p.m. of the same afternoon; autocorrelation hands it the answers through the wall. The cure is to split the way deployment splits: *forward in time*, train on the past, score on the future.

```{python}
#| label: fig-leakage
#| fig-cap: "The same model, two evaluation designs. Random folds reward the model for memorizing the neighborhood of each hour; forward-chaining tells the truth about forecasting."
#| code-fold: true
# TODO:data — shuffled K-fold vs TimeSeriesSplit on identical model/features;
# paired bar or dot plot of MAE
```

<!-- TODO:data — state the actual optimism gap, e.g. "random folds flatter the model by X%" -->

Space leaks exactly as time does. Add a feature like *the count at the nearest other sensor, same hour* and watch the scores soar — the model has discovered that adjacent streets are simultaneously busy, which is geography, not foresight, and unavailable when forecasting next week. The general rule survives every special case: **evaluation must rehearse deployment.** Decide what the model will genuinely know at the moment of use, and permit it nothing else at the moment of judgment. When @sec-spatial formalizes spatial dependence, and when @sec-causal builds entire research designs out of what-was-knowable-when, this rule will already be an old friend.

Leakage is the field's polite word for grading yourself with the answer key in hand. The grade always comes out well, and means nothing.

::: {.callout-note}
## The clipboard before the sensor

Melbourne did not start counting pedestrians because sensors became cheap. It started because in 1994 the Danish architect Jan Gehl — heir to William Whyte's New York street-corner filmography of the 1970s — was hired to survey public life in a city center then so deserted after hours that locals called it "the doughnut": busy rim, empty middle. Gehl's teams counted by hand, clipboard and tally, the methods of his decades of Copenhagen studies. The 1994 numbers shamed the city; the follow-up in 2004 measured a renaissance — café seats tripled, evening foot traffic up by half — and made Melbourne the global poster child for measured, deliberate public-life repair. The sensor network, switched on in 2009, is that clipboard tradition automated and made permanent.

The lineage is worth remembering when the machine learning gets absorbing. Whyte filmed plazas to learn *why* people stay — the sittable ledge, the sun, the other people. Gehl counted to convict a city of neglecting its public rooms and then to certify the repair. The sensors count magnificently and explain nothing; the explaining is still done the old way, by someone standing in the street, watching. The dataset is the heir of a humanism, and it has not outgrown its parents.
:::

A counting machine bolted above a shopping street is an unglamorous instrument, and sixteen years of its output have now carried a chapter. That is the general lesson, and it compounds: the patient sensor beats the clever snapshot, in cities as in astronomy. Melbourne decided in 2009 that attention to its streets was worth automating, and every analysis in this chapter — the forecasts, the street personalities, the canyon and the climb back out — was interest paid on that decision.

The next chapter keeps the habit of suspicion and adds a dimension we have been treating as a nuisance. The sensors disagreed with each other *in space*; streets resembled their neighbors; geography kept trying to leak into the models. In @sec-spatial, space stops being a leak and becomes the subject.

## Exercises {.unnumbered}

1. **Beat the chapter.** Using any model and any honestly-available features, improve on the boosted model's test MAE at the anchor sensor — same forward-in-time split, no peeking. Report your error, your baseline's, and the hour-of-week where your model fails worst, with a hypothesis for why.
2. **The uneven recovery.** Compute each cluster's 2025 traffic as a share of its 2019 level. Which street personalities recovered and which did not? Write the one-paragraph memo a city economist would actually want, including the number you trust least.
3. **The strange day.** Find the most anomalous non-pandemic day in the record and identify the real-world event behind it. Newspapers are admissible evidence. If you find a day you *cannot* explain, you have found something better; document it.
4. **Weather, honestly.** Add rainfall and temperature from the Bureau of Meteorology — as a deployed forecaster would have them, which is to say as *forecasts*, or failing that, lagged observations only. Report the improvement and whether it survives the honesty constraint.
5. **The next sensor.** The city can afford five more sensors. Propose locations, the question each would answer, and — the part that separates analysts from vendors — the bias your placement scheme builds into every future citywide statistic.

## Further reading {.unnumbered}

- **Breiman, "Statistical Modeling: The Two Cultures" (2001).** The polemic this chapter's framing borrows; read it with the published discussions, where the other culture answers back.
- **Shmueli, "To Explain or to Predict?" (2010).** The cooler-headed companion piece; the clearest statement of why the goals demand different practices.
- **Hyndman & Athanasopoulos, *Forecasting: Principles and Practice* (3rd ed., free online).** The forecasting craft in full, including the baselines this chapter weaponized.
- **Gehl & Svarre, *How to Study Public Life* (2013).** The clipboard tradition by its living master; pairs with Whyte's 1980 film and book.
- **Molnar, *Interpretable Machine Learning* (free online).** What importance plots and their relatives do and do not license you to say.
